title: 2 Samuel 16:15–23
context: Absalom enters Jerusalem with Ahithophel. Hushai greets him with "Long live the king!" and wins his trust with carefully ambiguous words of loyalty. Absalom then asks Ahithophel for counsel, and Ahithophel advises a public act meant to make the break with David irreversible: Absalom takes his father's concubines in a tent on the roof in the sight of all Israel. The narrator records this as the fulfillment of Nathan's word in 2 Samuel 12:11–12, and notes how highly Ahithophel's counsel was regarded.

verses.text: Absalom and all the people, the men of Israel, came to Jerusalem, and Ahithophel with him.
verses.arminianNotes: Absalom and the men of Israel enter Jerusalem with Ahithophel. Arminian readers see the apparent success of a rebellion built on deceit, and note that outward success does not mean God's approval.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Absalom now holds the city, yet God's purpose has not changed. The rebel's moment of triumph is the stage on which God will overturn his counsel.

verses.text: When Hushai the Archite, David’s friend, had come to Absalom, Hushai said to Absalom, “Long live the king! Long live the king!”
verses.arminianNotes: Hushai cries, "Long live the king!" Arminian readers note the ambiguity: Hushai never names which king, a careful choice of words that serves his mission while avoiding a direct lie.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also note the deliberate ambiguity. Hushai's words can be heard as loyal to David while Absalom hears them as loyalty to himself, and God uses this to answer David's prayer.

verses.text: Absalom said to Hushai, “Is this your kindness to your friend? Why didn’t you go with your friend?”
verses.arminianNotes: "Is this your kindness to your friend?" Absalom questions Hushai's loyalty. Arminian readers note the irony that Absalom, who betrayed his own father, now questions another man's faithfulness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the irony that Absalom accuses Hushai of disloyalty while committing far worse treachery himself. Sin often sees in others what it refuses to see in itself.

verses.text: Hushai said to Absalom, “No; but whomever the LORD and this people and all the men of Israel have chosen, I will be his, and I will stay with him.
verses.arminianNotes: "Whomever the LORD and this people and all the men of Israel have chosen, I will be his." Arminian readers note that Hushai's words are true in a sense Absalom does not grasp: the LORD's chosen king is David.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Hushai's statement rings true for David, whom God chose. His double meaning points to a reality Absalom cannot see: God's choice, not popular acclaim, determines the true king.

verses.text: Again, whom should I serve? Shouldn’t I serve in the presence of his son? As I have served in your father’s presence, so I will be in your presence.”
verses.arminianNotes: "As I have served in your father's presence, so I will be in your presence." Arminian readers see Hushai playing his role carefully, serving David's cause through a dangerous deception.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Hushai positions himself in Absalom's court as God's instrument. The ethics of his deception are debated, but the narrative presents him as David's faithful friend.

verses.text: Then Absalom said to Ahithophel, “Give your counsel what we shall do.”
verses.arminianNotes: Absalom asks Ahithophel for counsel. Arminian readers note that Absalom seeks human wisdom rather than God's guidance, and that the counsel he receives will deepen his rebellion.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Absalom turns to Ahithophel, not to God. His reliance on human counsel sets up the contrast with 17:14, where God overturns even the best human advice.

verses.text: Ahithophel said to Absalom, “Go in to your father’s concubines that he has left to keep the house. Then all Israel will hear that you are abhorred by your father. Then the hands of all who are with you will be strong.”
verses.arminianNotes: Ahithophel advises Absalom to take his father's concubines so that the break with David becomes public and permanent. Arminian readers see calculated evil, counsel designed to make reconciliation impossible.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the act was a public claim to the throne and an irreversible insult to David. Ahithophel's shrewd but wicked counsel serves to fulfill God's word of judgment (12:11).

verses.text: So they spread a tent for Absalom on the top of the house, and Absalom went in to his father’s concubines in the sight of all Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: A tent is spread on the roof, and Absalom goes in to the concubines "in the sight of all Israel." Arminian readers see the bitter fruit of David's own sin returning on his house, a grievous wrong done to these women.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the exact fulfillment of 12:11–12, where God said, "I will do this thing before all Israel." David's secret sin is answered by public shame, and the narrator records it with restraint.

verses.text: The counsel of Ahithophel, which he gave in those days, was as if a man inquired at the inner sanctuary of God. All the counsel of Ahithophel was like this both with David and with Absalom.
verses.arminianNotes: Ahithophel's counsel was regarded "as if a man inquired at the inner sanctuary of God." Arminian readers note the danger of treating human wisdom as divine, especially when it serves rebellion.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that this high regard sets up the reversal of 17:14. Even counsel likened to God's word cannot stand against God's own purpose, and Ahithophel's end (17:23) shows its limits.
